$comment: The declared half of the dashboard's data. The other half is derived from
the repository by scripts/generate.mjs, which also VALIDATES this file:
every test named below must exist as a real Go test function, every file
must exist, and every enum value must be known. The build fails otherwise.
That is what stops this file becoming a second place to write things that
are not true. It cannot stop a wrong summary being written next to a real
test name -- nothing can -- but it does stop a guarantee citing evidence
declared - written by a human here, reference-checked by the generator
derived  - computed from the repository at build time
ci       - snapshot of a CI run, carries its own timestamp
runtime  - only knowable on a host running Nim; never available here

project.name: Nim
project.tagline: A local process between an MCP client and the MCP servers it uses.
project.currentPhase: Agent identity — enrolment and derivation landed; policy not started
project.statusNote: Nim decides, blocks and records. It has no policy model beyond a list of tool names, and agent identity is recorded but not yet acted on.

ciSnapshot.$comment: Snapshot, not live. Staleness is computed against the commit being built.

runtime.$comment: Deliberately empty. See the note rendered on the Overview.
runtime.reason: Nim is local-first. The journal, enrolled agents, connectors and the daemon all live on the machine running Nim. A hosted page cannot see them, and shipping them to one would break the sync contract in docs/milestones.md. `nim console` serves that state over loopback, which is where it belongs.

nodes.label: MCP client
nodes.note: Spawns one relay per configured server. Its own executable is what an agent identity is derived from.

nodes.label: nim serve
nodes.note: Forwards every byte untouched. Asks the daemon before forwarding a tools/call and waits.

nodes.label: nim daemon
nodes.note: Decides, holds credentials, owns SQLite. Verifies its peers and is verified by them.

nodes.label: MCP server
nodes.note: Untrusted by assumption: code the operator did not write, running as the same user.

nodes.label: Remote resource
nodes.note: Outside Nim entirely. Nim never sees this hop.

layers.name: Agent identity
layers.detail: Enrolled and derived from the kernel, recorded on session.start. Nothing decides on it yet.

layers.name: Policy
layers.detail: A deny list of exact tool names, read from config.toml. Not per-agent, and anything able to write that file can empty it.

layers.name: Credential access
layers.detail: Secrets in the OS store, released only for the connector's registered command.

layers.name: Peer verification
layers.detail: Both ends of the socket verify each other by kernel-resolved executable identity. Unsupported on Windows.

layers.name: Journal
layers.detail: Append-only and hash-chained. Integrity, not authenticity — the chain is unkeyed.

layers.name: SQLite
layers.detail: Source of truth for the journal, connectors and agents. The only thing an authorization decision should read.

guarantees.title: Both ends of the daemon socket verify each other
guarantees.statement: A process that is not this binary cannot speak on the daemon socket, in either direction. The daemon checks its callers and the relay checks whatever is listening before sending a byte.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: It answers "is this Nim", not "is this a relay the operator meant to run". Anything able to execute the binary passes it.

guarantees.title: Peer identity is the running image, not a filename
guarantees.statement: Identity comes from the kernel's view of what a process is executing: /proc/<pid>/exe on linux, the vnode behind the process's own mapping on darwin. Replacing the file at a peer's launch path does not defeat it.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: It is not code-signing identity. A rebuild is a different inode and therefore a different program. Not implemented on Windows at all.

guarantees.title: A credential is only injected into the command it was registered for
guarantees.statement: A connector names the one server its secret may reach. The daemon returns that command; the relay spawns it. A caller naming another connector gets that connector's real server, which is not a way to read anything.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: The registered argv is spawned through normal PATH resolution, so a caller that already controls PATH can front-run the binary name.

guarantees.title: A secret never becomes a command-line argument
guarantees.statement: Secrets are read from stdin or a no-echo prompt, stored in the OS credential store, and reach a connector only through its environment.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: The connector receives the secret in its environment and can do what it likes with it. On Linux any same-user process can read /proc/<pid>/environ.

guarantees.title: Every way of not getting a decision is a denial
guarantees.statement: No daemon, a slow daemon, a closed socket, a reply that does not match the question, or a journal write that failed — each denies. There is no path on which a tools/call reaches a connector without a decision behind it.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: It protects calls that go through Nim. Nothing stops a client being reconfigured to spawn the MCP server directly.

guarantees.title: The journal is append-only in fact, not by convention
guarantees.statement: A call produces two immutable entries rather than one row that is updated. Nothing in the write path updates an entry.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: Append-only as far as this code is concerned. Nothing stops another process opening the file and writing to it.

guarantees.title: Altering an entry breaks the chain
guarantees.statement: Each entry's hash covers its contents and its position, so an edit made by anything that does not recompute the chain is detected by nim verify.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: INTEGRITY, NOT AUTHENTICITY. The chain is unkeyed. Anyone who can write to nim.db can recompute every hash from the genesis and the result verifies cleanly.

guarantees.title: A recorded head detects truncate-and-recompute
guarantees.statement: nim verify --expect-head looks for the recorded head IN the chain. Finding it establishes that nothing at or before it was rewritten; not finding it anywhere is what distinguishes a rewrite from ordinary growth.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: Only covers what was committed before the head you recorded, and only if you recorded one somewhere Nim cannot reach.

guarantees.title: A journal spanning schema versions still verifies
guarantees.statement: Verification dispatches on the version each entry stored, so entries written before agent existed keep verifying and a mixed chain checks out end to end.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: An entry claiming a version this build does not know is refused rather than checked. That is intended, but it means a downgrade cannot read a newer journal.

guarantees.title: An agent identity cannot be claimed by the agent
guarantees.statement: The daemon derives the agent from the kernel: socket peer, its parent, the file that parent executes. There is no agent field on the wire.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: Nothing decides on it yet. Two windows of one program are the same agent. Enrolment is as privileged as running Nim.

guarantees.title: A connection may only speak for sessions it opened
guarantees.statement: Peer identity cannot tell one run of Nim from another; session ownership stops one connection appending entries under a session another opened.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: Anything running this binary can still open its own session and report whatever it likes about it.

guarantees.title: A client cannot tell it is going through Nim
guarantees.statement: Everything that is not a tools/call is forwarded as the exact bytes that arrived. Unit tests cover the framing and the relay.
guarantees.notGuaranteed: The end-to-end proof is tools/relay-rig, which needs fastmcp and HAS NOT BEEN RE-RUN since the M1.5 merge. The claim currently rests on unit tests plus an older run.

attacks.name: Name a connector, supply your own command, read the credential
attacks.evidence: Reproduced live against a real build; the token printed. Fixed by the connector command binding.

attacks.name: Ask for a credential from a process that is not Nim
attacks.evidence: Raw socket client denied.

attacks.name: Write forged entries to the journal from a non-Nim process
attacks.evidence: A python socket client wrote a fabricated session and an allowed delete_repository call. Fixed by authorizing the event path.

attacks.name: Obtain a decision from a non-Nim process
attacks.evidence: Connection closed before any decision is produced.

attacks.name: Report calls under a session another connection opened
attacks.evidence: Refused; the connection is closed.

attacks.name: Bind the socket first and impersonate the daemon
attacks.evidence: As the daemon, a python script had the relay spawn a command of its choosing, allowed a denied call, and harvested tool names. Introduced by the merge; fixed by verifying both ends.

attacks.name: As an impostor, harvest tool names and argument digests
attacks.evidence: Verification happens before a byte is written, so the impostor learns nothing.

attacks.name: Defeat peer identity by swapping the file at the peer's launch path
attacks.evidence: A genuine nc process passed peer identity with no race. Fixed by resolving the running image instead of a path. Mutation-verified.

attacks.name: Exhaust daemon memory with an unterminated line
attacks.evidence: 200 MiB in 0.2s from one unauthenticated connection. Capped at 1 MiB.

attacks.name: Bypass the deny list
attacks.evidence: Denied call never reaches the connector.

attacks.name: Smuggle a tools/call inside a JSON-RPC batch
attacks.evidence: Batch carrying a tools/call is refused whole.

attacks.name: Smuggle a call in a frame Go cannot parse but the server can
attacks.evidence: Unreadable frames are not relayed.

attacks.name: Kill the daemon to disable enforcement
attacks.evidence: Every call denied.

attacks.name: Truncate the journal's tail
attacks.evidence: Detected ONLY with --expect-head against a head recorded elsewhere. Undetectable otherwise, because the chain is unkeyed.

attacks.name: Rewrite the whole journal from the genesis
attacks.evidence: Not defended. Nothing in the chain is secret, so anyone who can write nim.db can recompute every hash and the result verifies cleanly. Only an externally recorded head covers any of it.

attacks.name: Pass --expect-head a head the journal has grown past
attacks.evidence: Previously reported ordinary growth as 'entries have been removed'. A check that cries wolf stops being read.

attacks.name: Claim an agent identity on the wire
attacks.evidence: There is no agent field on Event; the serialised message is asserted not to contain one.

attacks.name: Use a stale enrolment after the executable is replaced
attacks.evidence: A replaced file no longer matches; the enrolment is reported STALE rather than silently adopting the new file.

attacks.name: Land a new file on a deleted enrolment's inode number
attacks.evidence: Inode reuse is real: ext4 hands back the number it just freed, observed in CI. A running process holds its inode so the runtime path is safe; a PERSISTED enrolment whose file was deleted could be matched by an unrelated later file. No test covers the adversarial case.

attacks.name: Overwrite another agent's enrolment
attacks.evidence: Anything that can run the nim binary as this user can re-enrol any name against any executable. Harmless today because nothing decides on agents; becomes an escalation the moment grants exist.

attacks.name: Overwrite a connector's registered command
attacks.evidence: Possible, but destructive rather than exfiltrating: connector.set requires a secret, so an attacker replaces the credential with their own rather than reading the existing one.

attacks.name: Front-run the registered command through PATH
attacks.evidence: The registered argv is spawned through normal PATH resolution. A caller that already controls PATH can place its own binary first. Closing it needs the daemon to spawn the connector itself.

attacks.name: Leave a connector running after the relay dies
attacks.evidence: The downstream is the relay's child and dies with it.

attacks.name: Restart the daemon mid-session
attacks.evidence: Sessions left open are closed by the daemon when a connection drops, and calls fail closed. Not exercised as a deliberate restart-under-load test.

attacks.name: Run a new client against an old daemon
attacks.evidence: Replacing the binary in place while a daemon runs breaks every operation until it is restarted, with an opaque 'reading response: EOF'. Fails closed, but the message tells the operator nothing.

attacks.name: Open the journal from two processes at once
attacks.evidence: Found by CI: syncViews dropped and recreated a view unsynchronised. Now one immediate transaction; regression test fails 5/5 against the old code.

attacks.name: Provoke races under contention
attacks.evidence: Three real races found and fixed with reproductions: split-brain daemon start, torn credential read, BUSY_SNAPSHOT. Suite runs -race -shuffle.

attacks.name: Feed the daemon malformed JSON
attacks.evidence: Malformed messages are recorded as an anomaly and skipped; oversized ones are refused before the full parse.

attacks.name: Reuse a JSON-RPC id for two in-flight calls
attacks.evidence: Recorded as a duplicate_id anomaly. The second answer still cannot be matched to the right request, and nothing prevents the situation.

attacks.name: Crash between decision and forward
attacks.evidence: No test. The known window is documented: the relay gives up after 2s and SQLite's busy timeout is 5s, so a contended write can land after a denial, leaving an allow for a call that never happened. It reads as pending, never as executed.

attacks.name: Crash while relaying a response
attacks.evidence: No test.

attacks.name: Power loss mid-commit
attacks.evidence: synchronous=FULL is asserted but never tested against real hardware loss.

attacks.name: Cross a privilege boundary
attacks.evidence: There is no privilege boundary to cross. Everything runs as one OS user by design; that is the premise, not a gap.

attacks.name: Act as an agent nobody enrolled
attacks.evidence: The recording behaviour is tested: an underivable agent is stored as absent, not refused. What an unknown agent may DO is undecided — that is M4's open question (D-002), not an answer inherited from here.

attacks.name: Name a connector that does not exist
attacks.evidence: No connector configured is the ordinary case: spawn with no credential.

attacks.name: Call a tool no policy mentions
attacks.evidence: Allowed. The deny list is a deny list, so anything not on it passes — deliberate for now, and the reason a real policy model is the next milestone.

attacks.name: A same-user process that already ran code
attacks.evidence: This is the threat model's adversary and it is only partly contained. It can run the nim binary, enrol agents, overwrite connectors, and open its own sessions. What it cannot do is read another connector's credential or forge entries without running Nim.

attacks.name: Manipulate symlinks and paths
attacks.evidence: The path-swap test builds the attack out of symlinks: it launches a peer through a symlink it controls, then re-points that symlink at Nim's own binary so the launch path names Nim while the running process is genuinely something else. Identity comes from the kernel's view of the running image, so the swap changes nothing.

attacks.name: Read a credential from the connector's environment
attacks.evidence: By design the connector receives the secret in its environment, and it inherits the relay's whole environment. On Linux any same-user process can read /proc/<pid>/environ. Closing it needs Nim to hold the credential and proxy the request.

attacks.name: Make this dashboard state something untrue
attacks.evidence: The generator refuses to build if a guarantee or attack cites a test that does not exist, or a file that is not in the repo. It cannot detect a wrong summary written next to a real test name.

findings.title: In-place upgrade breaks a running daemon, opaquely
findings.problem: Replacing the binary while a daemon runs makes the old daemon and the new client different images, so every operation is refused.
findings.impact: All Nim operations fail until the daemon is restarted. The client sees 'nim: reading response: EOF' with no hint.
findings.evidence: Reproduced live: daemon logs 'refusing a connection from an unverified peer'; the client sees EOF.
findings.nextAction: A version/identity handshake so the daemon can say 'I am an older build, restart me' instead of hanging up.

findings.title: Windows has no peer verification and no real ACL
findings.problem: AF_UNIX on Windows exposes no peer-credential API, and os.Chmod only toggles the read-only attribute.
findings.impact: On Windows, nothing verifies that a caller is Nim, and socket confidentiality rests on default directory ACLs.
findings.evidence: engine/internal/peer/image_windows.go returns unsupported by design. Nothing in this project has ever been run on Windows.
findings.nextAction: A named-pipe transport with GetNamedPipeClientProcessId and an explicit DACL — a real architecture change.

findings.title: The journal chain is unkeyed
findings.problem: Nothing in the chain is secret, so anyone able to write nim.db can recompute every hash from the genesis.
findings.impact: A local attacker can rewrite history and the result verifies cleanly. This is integrity, not authenticity.
findings.evidence: docs/journal-format.md states it. --expect-head is the only cover, and only for what was committed before the head you recorded.
findings.nextAction: Decide before M8: a key the agent cannot reach, or a dashboard that presents the record as 'what this machine reported'.

findings.title: Policy lives in config.toml
findings.problem: The deny list is read from a file, breaking the standing decision that SQLite is the only thing an authorization decision reads.
findings.impact: Anything able to write that file can empty the policy, and the change leaves no journal entry.
findings.evidence: engine/internal/config/config.go documents it as deliberate, temporary scaffolding.
findings.nextAction: Move policy into SQLite and journal every policy change. This is M4.

findings.title: A credential is handed to the connector
findings.problem: The secret is injected into the downstream's environment, and the downstream inherits the relay's whole environment.
findings.impact: A compromised connector has its own credential and cannot be revoked. On Linux any same-user process can read it from /proc.
findings.nextAction: Process inversion: the daemon spawns the connector and holds the credential.

findings.title: Enrolment is as privileged as running Nim
findings.problem: Anything that can execute the binary as this user can enrol an agent or replace an existing enrolment.
findings.impact: Harmless today because nothing decides on agents. It becomes an escalation the moment grants exist.
findings.evidence: engine/internal/daemon/agent.go says so in its own comment.
findings.nextAction: M4 must state what an enrolment is worth before grants are attached to one.

findings.title: The relay rig has not been re-run since M1.5
findings.problem: The end-to-end proof that a real client cannot tell it is going through Nim requires fastmcp, which is not installed here.
findings.impact: Byte-exactness currently rests on unit tests plus a run from before the merge.
findings.nextAction: Install fastmcp and re-run, or add it to CI.

findings.title: Socket permissions have a window at creation
findings.problem: net.Listen creates the socket with the process umask; chmod 0600 follows immediately after.
findings.impact: A brief window where the socket is connectable by other local users. Peer verification still refuses them.
findings.nextAction: Set a restrictive umask around the Listen call.

findings.title: CI does not run go vet for Windows
findings.problem: Cross-compile jobs run go build only, so test files that break on Windows are not caught.
findings.impact: A portability break in test code reaches main. This happened once already.
findings.evidence: Found by running GOOS=windows go vet locally during M4 step 2.
findings.nextAction: Add GOOS=windows go vet ./... to the cross-compile job.

findings.title: CI cannot show whether the path-swap test ran or skipped
findings.problem: CI does not pass -v, so a skipped adversarial test is indistinguishable from a passing one in the log.
findings.impact: The single test proving the peer-identity property could silently stop running.
findings.evidence: The ubuntu log shows only 'ok internal/peer'.
findings.nextAction: Add -v to the CI test step, or promote the connect-timeout skip to a failure.

decisions.title: What granularity is an 'agent'?
decisions.question: Client program (kernel-backed, coarse) or workspace/instance (finer, forgeable by the same user)?
decisions.resolution: Client program. Kernel-backed and honest; two windows of one program are the same agent.

decisions.title: What may an unknown agent do?
decisions.question: Once grants exist, is an unenrolled spawner denied, or does it fall back to the global policy?
decisions.resolution: Undecided. If 'not enrolled' were more permissive, enrolling would be a downgrade and an attacker would simply avoid it.

decisions.title: Should the hosted dashboard be publicly reachable?
decisions.question: It lists known weaknesses and attack paths for a private repository.
decisions.resolution: Undecided. Vercel Authentication or password protection would keep it to the team.

decisions.title: Does the journal get a key before M8?
decisions.question: Syncing an unkeyed record to a dashboard exports a liability rather than evidence.
decisions.resolution: Undecided. Either the journal gains a key the agent cannot reach, or M8 presents the record as 'what this machine reported'.

milestones.name: Pass-through
milestones.objective: Relay stdio byte-for-byte and record every tools/call.
limitations: Nothing blocked, no credentials, no policy.

milestones.name: Trustworthy record
milestones.objective: Make the journal evidence rather than a log.
limitations: Integrity, not authenticity. The chain is unkeyed.

milestones.name: Minimal enforcement
milestones.objective: Refuse a tools/call before it reaches a connector.
limitations: Policy is a list of exact tool names in config.toml.

milestones.name: Daemon lifetime and socket identity
milestones.objective: A daemon that outlives a client session, and a socket where both ends know who the other is.

milestones.name: Credentials
milestones.objective: Hold connector credentials outside the client's configuration.
limitations: PATH resolution on the registered command.
The credential is handed to the connector.

milestones.name: Agent identity + policy in SQLite
milestones.objective: Give a decision a subject, and move policy where an authorization input belongs.
limitations: Nothing decides on the agent yet.
Two windows of one program are the same agent.
pending: Decide what an unknown agent may do (D-002).

milestones.name: Grants (Cedar), if it is still the answer
milestones.objective: Express allow/deny in something richer than a list, once there is a subject to talk about.
pending: Deferred until M4 gives it a subject.

milestones.name: Budgets
milestones.objective: Per session, decremented at authorization time.

milestones.name: Journal
milestones.objective: Append-only, hash-chained, with the inputs that produced each decision.
limitations: The 'inputs that produced each decision' part folds into M4.

milestones.name: Dashboard
milestones.objective: A hosted view of the journal.
limitations: Blocked on the journal being unkeyed (F-003): syncing it exports a liability rather than evidence.
